cue: Describe a time when you worked in a team.
bullets: and explain how you felt about working in this team
part3: What makes some teams more successful than others?
Is it better for children to learn in groups or individually?
Should leaders be chosen by the team or appointed by someone senior?
How has remote working affected teamwork?
Do you think competition or cooperation is more useful at work?
modelAnswer: I'd like to talk about a group project I did in my final year at university, where four of us had to design a small survey and present our findings to a panel of lecturers. The team was a bit of a mixed bag: one person was extremely organised, another was brilliant with data but quite shy, and the fourth member was rather laid-back and tended to leave things until the last minute. I ended up taking on the role of coordinator, partly because nobody else wanted to, and partly because I'm quite good at keeping track of deadlines. I set up a shared calendar, split the work according to people's strengths and arranged short weekly check-ins. There were a few tense moments, especially when one section was handed in late, but we talked it through rather than letting it turn into an argument. Overall, I felt it was a really rewarding experience. We got a good mark, but more importantly I learned that a team works best when people's differences are treated as an advantage rather than a problem.
band6: I want to talk about a group project in my university. We were four students and we must make a survey and then present the result to the teachers. The people in my team were very different. One girl was very organised, one boy was good at statistics but he is shy, and another boy was lazy and always late. I was the leader because nobody want to do it and I am good with deadlines. I made a calendar online and I gave everyone a part of the work. Sometimes we had problems, for example one person sent his part late, but we talked and we solved it. In general I felt good in this team. We got a good mark and I learned that different people can work together well if everyone do their part.

notes.fc: Band 6 is easy to follow but moves through points mechanically. Band 7 signals the structure ('partly because... and partly because', 'Overall', 'but more importantly') and develops the conflict instead of just naming it.
notes.lr: Band 7: 'a bit of a mixed bag', 'laid-back', 'keeping track of', 'talked it through'. Band 6 uses 'lazy' and 'good' where more precise or tactful words would fit.
notes.gra: Band 6: 'we must make' (for past obligation), 'he is shy' in a past narrative, 'nobody want', 'everyone do'. Band 7 uses passive ('was handed in'), gerund phrases and contrast with 'rather than' accurately.
notes.pron: Band 7 delivery uses sentence stress to show contrast: 'treated as an ADVANTAGE rather than a PROBLEM'. Practise holding the stress on content words and reducing 'as an' and 'than a'.

cue: Describe a habit you would like to change.
bullets: how long you have had it
why you want to change it
and explain how you plan to change it
part3: Why is it so difficult for people to break bad habits?
Are habits formed in childhood harder to change than those formed later?
Should governments try to change people's habits, for example by taxing sugar?
How do advertisements influence people's habits?
Which good habits should schools teach children?
modelAnswer: The habit I'd really like to change is checking my phone the moment I wake up. I think it started around four years ago, when I began using my phone as an alarm clock, and gradually it became automatic. Before I've even got out of bed, I've usually scrolled through messages, news headlines and social media, which can easily take twenty minutes. The main reason I want to stop is that it puts me in a reactive frame of mind for the whole day. If I see a stressful email or a piece of bad news first thing, it tends to colour my mood, and I've noticed I'm less focused on the things I'd actually planned to do. It also makes me late more often than I'd like to admit. My plan is fairly simple. I've bought an ordinary alarm clock, and I'm going to charge my phone in the kitchen overnight so it isn't within reach. I also want to replace the habit with something better, such as stretching for five minutes or reading a few pages of a book before I look at a screen.
band6: A habit I want to change is that I look at my phone immediately when I wake up. I think I have this habit for about four years, since I use the phone for my alarm. Now every morning I check my messages, news and social media in the bed, and sometimes it is twenty minutes. I want to change because it makes me stressed. If I read a bad email or bad news in the morning, I feel bad all day, and I cannot focus on my work. Also I am late sometimes because of this. So my plan is to buy a normal alarm clock and to put my phone in the kitchen in the night. Then I will do some exercise or read a book in the morning, not look at the phone. I hope this plan will work.

notes.fc: Band 6 covers all bullets with simple sequencing. Band 7 explains the effect in more depth ('puts me in a reactive frame of mind', 'tends to colour my mood') so each point is extended, not just stated.
notes.lr: Band 6 repeats 'bad' three times. Band 7 uses idiomatic and precise language: 'first thing', 'within reach', 'more often than I'd like to admit'.
notes.gra: Band 6: 'I have this habit for about four years' (needs present perfect), 'since I use', 'in the bed'. Band 7 uses present perfect with 'Before I've even got out of bed', conditionals and purpose clauses accurately.
notes.pron: Practise the weak forms in 'I've usually', 'I'd like to admit' and linking 'first thing'. Band 6 speakers often drop contractions entirely, which makes the speech sound stilted.

cue: Describe a building in your city that you think is attractive.
bullets: and explain why you think it is attractive
part3: Should old buildings be preserved, or replaced with modern ones?
Who should pay for the upkeep of historic buildings?
How does the design of a building affect the people who use it?
Do you think modern cities all look too similar?
Should architects consider the environment more than appearance?
modelAnswer: The building I find most attractive in my city is the central library, which stands on a corner of the main square, opposite the town hall. It was built about ten years ago, and at first a lot of people criticised it because it looked so different from the older buildings around it. From the outside it's a tall, glass-fronted building with a roof that slopes down towards the square, and the lower floors are partly covered in wooden panels, which soften the overall effect. Inside there's a huge open atrium with stairs that wind up through the middle, and every floor has wide windows looking out over the city. Apart from books, it's used for exhibitions, language classes and community events, and there's a café on the ground floor that's always busy. I think it's attractive because it manages to be modern without feeling cold. The use of wood and natural light makes it very welcoming, and it's designed so that you can see people reading and studying from the street, which I think sends a positive message about learning.
band6: The building I like is the central library in my city. It is on the main square, near the town hall. It is quite new, maybe ten years old, and in the beginning many people did not like it because it is very different from the old buildings. Outside there is a lot of glass and also some wood, and the roof goes down to the square. Inside there is a big open space and stairs in the middle, and you can see the city from the windows. People go there for borrowing books, but also for exhibitions and classes, and there is a café which is always full. I think it is beautiful because it is modern but it is not cold, the wood and the light make it warm. And from the street you can see people studying, I like that.

notes.fc: Band 6 lists features but the final reason is added as an afterthought ('I like that'). Band 7 links the design features to the reason, using 'which I think sends a positive message' to finish the argument.
notes.lr: Band 7 uses precise architectural vocabulary: 'glass-fronted', 'atrium', 'wind up through the middle', 'soften the overall effect'. Band 6 says 'a big open space', 'goes down'.
notes.gra: Band 6: 'because it is very different' (past context), 'go there for borrowing books'. Band 7 uses passive ('was built', 'is used', 'is designed so that') and non-defining relative clauses accurately.
notes.pron: Stress the contrast 'modern without feeling cold'. Practise the word stress in 'architecture', 'exhibition' and 'atrium', which are often misplaced.

cue: Describe a time when you taught someone something.
bullets: and explain how you felt about the experience
part3: What qualities make a good teacher?
Is it better to learn practical skills from a teacher or from online videos?
Should older people be encouraged to learn new technology?
Do you think teachers should be paid more?
How will teaching change in the future?
modelAnswer: I'd like to talk about the time I taught my grandmother how to make video calls on a tablet. It was during a period when the family couldn't visit her for several months, and she was feeling quite isolated, so my parents bought her a tablet and asked me to help her use it. At first it was harder than I expected. She'd never used a touchscreen before, and things that seem obvious to me, like swiping or knowing which icon to press, were completely new to her. So I slowed right down. I wrote simple step-by-step instructions on a card in large handwriting, with little drawings of each icon, and we practised the same call over and over again, first with me sitting next to her and then with me calling from the next room. After about a week she could do it on her own, and soon she was calling relatives I hardly ever speak to myself. I felt really proud, but also a bit humbled, because it showed me how much patience good teaching requires, and how easy it is to forget what it's like to be a complete beginner.
band6: I will talk about when I taught my grandmother to do video calls. At that time we could not visit her for some months and she was lonely, so my parents bought her a tablet and I helped her. It was more difficult than I think. She never used a touchscreen before, so she did not know how to swipe or which button she has to press. So I went very slowly. I wrote the steps on a card with big letters and small pictures, and we practised many times. First I was next to her and then I called her from another room. After one week she can do it alone, and then she started to call all the family. I felt very proud of her. Also I understood that teaching needs a lot of patience, it is not easy.

notes.fc: Band 6 is coherent but the ending is short and general ('it is not easy'). Band 7 reflects on the experience with a two-part conclusion, showing the speaker can keep going and develop ideas.
notes.lr: Band 7: 'isolated', 'slowed right down', 'over and over again', 'humbled', 'a complete beginner'. Band 6 uses 'lonely' and 'button' acceptably but with less range.
notes.gra: Band 6: 'more difficult than I think', 'She never used' (needs past perfect), 'she has to press', 'she can do it alone'. Band 7 uses past perfect, comparison and 'how much patience good teaching requires' accurately.
notes.pron: The band 7 answer has long sentences; practise breathing at commas and keeping a steady rhythm. Stress 'slowed RIGHT DOWN' and 'over and OVER again' for natural emphasis.

cue: Describe a time when you were surprised by something.
bullets: and explain why it surprised you
part3: Do people generally like surprises, or do they prefer to know what will happen?
Is it a good idea to organise surprise parties?
Why do some news stories surprise people more than others?
How can unexpected events help people grow?
Do you think life is less surprising now that information is so easy to find?
modelAnswer: One thing that genuinely surprised me happened last winter, when I went to a small jazz concert with a colleague. It was in a basement venue in the city centre, and to be honest I only went because she had a spare ticket. Halfway through the evening, the bandleader announced that a guest would be joining them, and to my astonishment it was my old maths teacher from secondary school, who walked on stage carrying a saxophone. I'd had no idea that he played any instrument at all. At school he'd always come across as rather strict and serious, and I'd never imagined him having a life outside the classroom, let alone performing in front of an audience. And he was brilliant. He played several solos and was clearly enjoying himself enormously. During the break I went up to say hello, and he laughed and admitted that very few of his students knew. I think it surprised me so much because it completely changed my picture of him, and it reminded me that we often judge people by the single role we see them in.
band6: I want to talk about a surprise last winter. My colleague had one more ticket for a jazz concert so I went with her. The concert was in a small place under the ground in the city centre. In the middle of the concert the leader of the band said there is a special guest, and it was my maths teacher from high school! He came with a saxophone. I never knew that he can play music. In school he was very strict and serious, so I could not imagine that he has a hobby like this. He played really well and he looked very happy. In the break I said hello to him and he laughed and said not many students know about it. It surprised me because I had a different idea about him, and now I know that people can be very different outside their job.

notes.fc: Both answers tell the story in order. Band 7 builds suspense ('Halfway through the evening', 'to my astonishment') and closes with a general insight; band 6 reaches the same point but in plainer steps.
notes.lr: Band 7: 'basement venue', 'come across as', 'let alone', 'judge people by the single role'. Band 6 says 'a small place under the ground', which shows a vocabulary gap being worked around.
notes.gra: Band 6 errors in reported speech and sequence: 'said there is', 'I never knew that he can play', 'not many students know'. Band 7 backshifts correctly and uses past perfect ('I'd had no idea', 'he'd always come across').
notes.pron: Use a higher pitch and pause before the surprise ('and to my astonishment... it was my old maths teacher'). Band 6 speakers often deliver the key moment at the same pitch as everything else.

cue: Describe a TV programme or online series you enjoy watching.
bullets: what it is called or what it is about
and explain why you enjoy watching it
part3: How have people's viewing habits changed with streaming services?
Do you think television has a positive or negative influence on children?
Should there be stricter controls on what is shown on television?
Why are reality programmes so popular?
Can documentaries be as educational as books?
modelAnswer: A series I really enjoy is a nature documentary series that follows a team of wildlife researchers working in remote parts of the world. Each episode focuses on a single animal or habitat, for instance snow leopards in the mountains or the coral reefs of a particular island. I came across it more or less by accident, when the streaming service I use recommended it after I'd watched a programme about volcanoes. I usually watch an episode on Sunday evenings, when I've finished everything for the week and want something calm but still interesting. What I like most about it is that it doesn't just show beautiful scenery. It also shows the scientists' day-to-day work, including the frustrating parts, like waiting for weeks in a hide without seeing anything. That makes it feel honest rather than staged. I've also learned a surprising amount from it, for example about how climate change is affecting migration patterns. And the photography is stunning, so it's a good reminder of how much of the natural world I've never seen and probably never will.

cue: Describe a time when you had to make a quick decision.
bullets: how quickly you had to decide
and explain how you felt about the decision afterwards
part3: Is it better to make decisions quickly or to take time to think?
Which jobs require people to make fast decisions?
Do you think young people today find it harder to make decisions?
Should children be allowed to make important decisions about their education?
How can too much choice make decisions more difficult?
modelAnswer: I'd like to describe a decision I had to make at an airport about three years ago. I was on my way to a friend's wedding, and my first flight was delayed so badly that I was certain to miss my connection. When I got to the airline desk, the agent told me I had two options: wait nine hours for the next direct flight, which would get me there after the ceremony, or take a flight leaving in twenty minutes to a different city and then catch an overnight bus. There was a queue of angry passengers behind me, so I had about thirty seconds to choose. I went for the second option, ran to the gate and only just made it. The bus journey was long and uncomfortable, and I arrived exhausted and slightly crumpled, but I was there in time to see my friend get married. Afterwards, I felt very relieved and quite proud of myself, because I'm normally someone who likes to weigh everything up carefully. It showed me that sometimes a decision that's good enough, made quickly, is better than a perfect one made too late.

cue: Describe a historical period or event you would like to learn more about.
bullets: what the period or event is
what you already know about it
how you would like to learn more
and explain why you are interested in it
part3: Why should young people study history?
Is it better to learn history from books, museums or films?
Do you think history is often presented in a biased way?
How important is it to preserve historical sites?
What can modern societies learn from past events?
modelAnswer: A period I'd like to know much more about is the early days of long-distance sea trade in Asia, roughly between the ninth and fifteenth centuries. What I know at the moment is fairly basic. I'm aware that merchants travelled huge distances by ship, carrying goods such as ceramics, spices and textiles, and that ports along the coast grew into wealthy, multicultural cities as a result. I also know that archaeologists have found shipwrecks with thousands of pieces of pottery still intact. I'd like to learn more in a few different ways. I'd love to visit a maritime museum where some of these wrecks are displayed, and I'd probably start by reading a well-written general history to get the bigger picture before going into detail. I'm interested in it mainly because it shows how connected the world was long before modern technology. People from very different cultures were trading, exchanging ideas and even intermarrying, and I find that a useful reminder that globalisation isn't really a new phenomenon, even though we often talk about it as if it were.

cue: Describe a person you know who is good at their job.
bullets: and explain why you think they are good at their job
part3: What makes someone a good employee?
Is talent or hard work more important for success at work?
Should people be paid according to how well they do their job?
Why do some people stay in jobs they do not enjoy?
How can employers help their staff develop new skills?
modelAnswer: The person I'd like to talk about is the pharmacist who runs a small pharmacy near my parents' home. Her name is Linh, and I've known her for more than ten years, because my family has always gone to her shop, and I even did a short work-experience placement there when I was at school. Obviously her job involves preparing prescriptions and selling medicines, but in practice she does much more than that. A lot of older people in the area go to her for advice before they'd ever consider booking an appointment with a doctor. I think she's exceptionally good at her job for a few reasons. Firstly, she's extremely careful. I've seen her phone a doctor to double-check a dose when something didn't look right. Secondly, she explains things clearly, without using jargon, and she always makes sure people understand when and how to take their medication. But what really stands out is how she remembers her customers. She'll ask an elderly man how his knee is or whether a child's cough has cleared up, so people feel that she genuinely cares about them.

cue: Describe an outdoor activity you did for the first time.
bullets: and explain how you felt about doing it
part3: Why do some people prefer outdoor activities to indoor ones?
Do children today spend enough time outdoors?
Should schools organise more outdoor trips?
Are extreme sports worth the risk?
How can cities encourage people to be more active outside?
modelAnswer: The activity I'd like to talk about is kayaking, which I tried for the first time last summer. A friend of mine had been doing it for years, and she kept telling me that I'd love it, so eventually I agreed to join her on a beginner's trip along a quiet river about an hour outside the city. There were six of us in the group, plus an instructor who spent the first half hour teaching us how to hold the paddle properly and, more importantly, what to do if the kayak tipped over. I have to admit that I was quite nervous at the start, because I'm not a particularly strong swimmer. For the first twenty minutes I kept going round in circles, which was a bit embarrassing, but once I got the hang of it I started to really enjoy it. The river was surrounded by forest, and it was so quiet that we could hear birds and the sound of the paddles in the water. I felt a real sense of achievement by the end of the day, and I've since been back three more times.

cue: Describe a rule at school or work that you think is important.
bullets: what happens if people break it
and explain why you think it is important
part3: Why do some people break rules?
Should schools have strict rules about how students dress?
Are rules at work more important than rules at school?
Who should decide the rules in a family?
Can too many rules make people less responsible?
modelAnswer: A rule I think is really important is one we had at my last workplace, which was a small design company. The rule was that nobody was allowed to send a document to a client without a second person checking it first. It applied to everything, from short emails with attached quotes to final designs. If someone broke the rule, there wasn't a formal punishment as such, but the manager would sit down with them and go through what could have gone wrong, and if it happened again it would be mentioned in their annual review. At first some people found it annoying, because it slowed things down, especially when deadlines were tight. However, I think it's important for several reasons. Most obviously, it caught a lot of mistakes, such as wrong prices or spelling errors in a client's name, which could have been really embarrassing. But it also meant that responsibility was shared, so nobody felt they had to be perfect on their own. And I think it encouraged people to learn from each other, because you often picked up useful ideas by checking someone else's work.

cue: Describe a time when you visited a friend or relative's home.
bullets: and explain how you felt about the visit
part3: How important is it for family members to visit each other regularly?
Do people entertain guests at home less than they used to?
What are the differences between visiting someone in a city and in the countryside?
Is it rude to arrive at someone's home without being invited?
How do customs for visiting someone's home differ between cultures?
modelAnswer: I'd like to describe a visit to my aunt's home in a small mountain village, which I went to for a long weekend last spring. It's about five hours from my city by bus, followed by a short drive up a winding road, so I don't get the chance to go very often. Her house is an old wooden building with a big vegetable garden at the back and a view across the valley. We didn't do anything particularly exciting, but that was part of the charm. In the mornings I helped her in the garden, picking herbs and planting beans, and in the afternoons we went for long walks or visited her neighbours, who all seemed to know who I was before I'd even introduced myself. In the evenings we cooked together and talked for hours about family stories I'd never heard before. I felt incredibly relaxed by the end of it. Living in a busy city, I'd almost forgotten what it was like to have no schedule at all, and the visit made me realise I should make more of an effort to see her.

cue: Describe a time when you saved money for something special.
bullets: and explain how you felt when you finally bought it
part3: Why do some people find it hard to save money?
Should schools teach children how to manage money?
Is it better to save money or to enjoy it now?
How has the way people pay for things changed in recent years?
Do you think buying on credit is a good idea?
modelAnswer: Something I saved up for that felt really special was a good-quality digital camera, which I bought when I was about nineteen. I'd become interested in photography at school, but I'd only ever used my phone, and I wanted a camera that would let me control the settings properly. The one I wanted was quite expensive, so it took me about eight months to save enough. I did it in a fairly disciplined way. I worked extra shifts at the café where I had a part-time job, and every time I got paid, I moved a fixed amount into a separate savings account before I could spend it. I also cut back on things like eating out and buying new clothes, which was harder than I expected, because my friends were going out a lot that year. When I finally went to the shop and bought it, I felt a huge sense of satisfaction, partly because it was the most expensive thing I'd ever bought with my own money. I think I've looked after it much more carefully as a result, and I still use it now.

cue: Describe a talk or lecture you found interesting.
bullets: and explain why you found it interesting
part3: Do you think lectures are still an effective way of teaching?
What makes a speaker interesting to listen to?
Should people learn public speaking at school?
Are online talks as useful as attending in person?
Why do some people feel nervous speaking in public?
modelAnswer: I'd like to talk about a guest lecture I attended during my first year at university, given by a researcher who studies how cities can adapt to rising temperatures. It was held in the main lecture theatre, which was packed because it was open to the public as well as to students. The talk was about what she called 'urban heat islands', which are areas of a city that become much hotter than the surrounding countryside because of concrete, asphalt and a lack of trees. She showed thermal images of the same street before and after trees had been planted, and the difference in surface temperature was quite dramatic. I found it interesting for a couple of reasons. Firstly, she explained a fairly technical subject in a way that anyone could follow, using everyday examples like why a car parked in the sun becomes so hot. Secondly, it was very practical. She talked about cheap solutions, such as painting roofs white and creating small green spaces, which made the problem feel solvable rather than hopeless. I've noticed shade and trees in my city much more since then.

cue: Describe a new skill you would like to learn in the future.
bullets: how long you think it would take
and explain why you want to learn this skill
part3: Is it easier to learn new skills as a child or as an adult?
Should employers pay for their staff to learn new skills?
Which skills will be most important in the future job market?
Do you think online courses are as effective as face-to-face classes?
Why do some people stop learning once they finish school?
modelAnswer: A skill I'd really like to learn in the next few years is basic woodworking, so that I can make and repair simple furniture. I'd probably start with an evening course at a community workshop near my home, because I don't have any tools of my own and I think it's important to learn how to use them safely from someone experienced. Later on, I'd supplement that with online videos and practise at home once I'd bought a few essential tools. As for how long it would take, I imagine I could make something simple, like a small shelf, within a couple of months, but to become genuinely skilled would probably take several years of regular practice. There are a few reasons why I want to learn it. Most of my work involves sitting at a computer, so I'm drawn to the idea of doing something physical where you can see the result of your effort. I also dislike how often furniture is thrown away when it could easily be repaired. And, on a personal level, I think it would be very satisfying to have things in my home that I'd made myself.
